segments.title: Three Mile Island and the Light That Said Closed
segments.summary: In 1979 a relief valve at Three Mile Island stuck open while a control-room light told operators it was closed. The light showed the command sent to the valve, not the valve's real position, and the reactor lost coolant for hours while people did what their instruments told them.
keyPoints: The indicator reported the command, not the valve's actual position
Operators acted rationally on wrong signals and cut back emergency cooling
Perrow: complex, tightly coupled systems make accidents normal, not freak events
segments.takeaway: A status light that reports intent instead of reality is worse than no light at all.
segments.challenge: Pick one green check in your monitoring and confirm whether it measures the real outcome or only that a command was sent.

source.title: Normal Accidents: Living with High-Risk Technologies
source.author: Charles Perrow

visual.title: What the panel said vs. what was real

items.label: Panel light
items.detail: Showed the 'close' command had been sent

items.label: Actual valve
items.detail: Stuck open, draining coolant for over two hours

visual.caption: Measure the valve, not the command.

script.speaker: host
script.text: Good morning, and welcome in. I'm Maya.

script.speaker: cohost
script.text: And I'm Theo. Today's thread is why good systems fail quietly, and how the signals we trust can lie to us.

script.speaker: host
script.text: Let's start in Pennsylvania, March 1979. Three Mile Island, Unit 2. Around four in the morning, pumps in the cooling system trip, pressure in the reactor climbs, and a relief valve pops open to let some of it out. Exactly as designed.

script.speaker: cohost
script.text: So far, so boring.

script.speaker: host
script.text: So far. The pressure drops, and the valve is supposed to close. It doesn't. It sticks open, and cooling water starts draining out of the system.

script.speaker: cohost
script.text: But surely there's a light for that.

script.speaker: host
script.text: There is a light. And the light says the valve is closed.

script.speaker: cohost
script.text: Wait. How?

script.speaker: host
script.text: Because the light didn't measure the valve. It measured the command. It showed that the control system had sent the signal to close. Nobody had wired it to the valve's actual position.

script.speaker: cohost
script.text: Oh, that's painful. So the dashboard was reporting intent, not reality.

script.speaker: host
script.text: Exactly. And other gauges suggested there was too much water, so the operators did the reasonable thing and throttled back the emergency cooling. For more than two hours the reactor lost coolant while the people in the room followed their instruments. The core partially melted.

script.speaker: cohost
script.text: The sociologist Charles Perrow wrote a whole book about this, called Normal Accidents. His argument is uncomfortable. When a system is complex enough that parts interact in ways nobody can see, and tightly coupled so one failure races into the next, accidents aren't freak events. They're normal. Built in.

script.speaker: host
script.text: And the operators weren't fools. They were buried in alarms, well over a hundred in the first few minutes, with one key indicator quietly wrong.

script.speaker: cohost
script.text: Which is a very familiar feeling if you've ever stared at a green status page in the middle of an outage.

script.speaker: host
script.text: Right. So here's the question for anyone who builds monitoring. For every status you trust, does it report what you asked for, or what actually happened? An interface that says admin up. A config push that says success. A health check that only proves the process is running.

script.speaker: cohost
script.text: Measure the valve, not the command.

script.speaker: host
script.text: Measure the valve, not the command. Hold onto that, because the next story starts with an airplane that was too much airplane.

deeperQuestions: Which of our health checks would stay green during a real outage?
Where are our systems tightly coupled enough that one fault cascades in minutes?
How would we know if an alarm flood is hiding the one signal that matters?

segments.title: The Crash That Invented the Checklist
segments.summary: In 1935 Boeing's Model 299, the future B-17, crashed on its demonstration flight because an expert pilot forgot to release a control lock. Instead of blaming the plane or the pilot, test pilots wrote a checklist, and the aircraft went on to fly about 1.8 million miles without an accident.
keyPoints: Experts rarely fail from ignorance; they miss steps under pressure
A short checklist turned 'too complex to fly' into routine
A 2009 WHO surgical checklist study cut deaths almost in half
segments.takeaway: When complexity outruns memory, the answer is a better checklist, not a better hero.
segments.challenge: Write the three 'killer steps' of your riskiest change procedure on one index card.

visual.title: From crash to checklist

items.label: Model 299 crashes
items.detail: Gust lock left on during takeoff

items.label: Pilots write a checklist
items.detail: Takeoff, flight, landing, taxi; fits an index card

items.label: Surgical checklist study
items.detail: Deaths fell about 47% across eight hospitals

visual.caption: The plane wasn't too hard to fly. It was too hard to remember.

script.speaker: host
script.text: October 1935, Wright Field in Ohio. The Army is holding a competition for a new long-range bomber, and Boeing's entry, the Model 299, is the clear favorite. Bigger, faster, longer range than anything else there.

script.speaker: cohost
script.text: And that becomes the B-17, right?

script.speaker: host
script.text: Eventually. On the demonstration flight it climbs to about three hundred feet, stalls, and crashes. Two of the men on board die.

script.speaker: cohost
script.text: Mechanical failure?

script.speaker: host
script.text: That's what you'd assume. It wasn't. The pilot, a very experienced test pilot named Ployer Hill, had forgotten to release a gust lock, a mechanism that holds the control surfaces still while the plane is parked. A newspaper called it too much airplane for one man to fly.

script.speaker: cohost
script.text: So the lesson everyone drew was, the system is too complex.

script.speaker: host
script.text: And Boeing lost the contract. But a group of test pilots drew a different lesson. The plane wasn't too hard to fly. It was too hard to remember. So they wrote a checklist. Step by step checks for takeoff, flight, landing and taxiing, small enough to fit on an index card.

script.speaker: cohost
script.text: That feels almost insultingly simple for expert pilots.

script.speaker: host
script.text: That's the point Atul Gawande makes in The Checklist Manifesto. Experts don't usually fail from ignorance. They fail from what he calls ineptitude. They know what to do and still miss a step under pressure. With the checklist, those pilots flew the Model 299 about one point eight million miles without a single accident.

script.speaker: cohost
script.text: And Gawande took the idea into surgery.

script.speaker: host
script.text: He did. In a World Health Organization study published in 2009, eight hospitals around the world tried a nineteen item surgical checklist. Deaths dropped by almost half. Major complications fell by about a third.

script.speaker: cohost
script.text: For us the parallel is the change runbook. Not because engineers are careless.

script.speaker: host
script.text: Because complexity outruns memory. And the good checklists are short. They cover the killer steps only, and they include a pause where the team actually talks and says what worries them.

script.speaker: cohost
script.text: So the checklist is secretly a conversation starter.

script.speaker: host
script.text: Which brings us to a doctor who had the data, and still lost the argument.

deeperQuestions: Which of our runbooks are really reference manuals pretending to be checklists?
What are the three steps that, if skipped, cause most of our change-related incidents?
Where would a deliberate team pause before a risky change catch problems?

segments.title: Semmelweis: The Doctor Who Had the Data and Lost
segments.summary: In 1840s Vienna, Ignaz Semmelweis showed that doctors coming from autopsies were spreading childbed fever, and handwashing cut deaths dramatically. He was ignored and mocked, partly because the message implicated the doctors themselves and partly because he delivered it terribly.
keyPoints: Two clinics in one hospital formed a natural experiment
Chlorine handwashing dropped deaths from about 10% to 1-2%
Being right wasn't enough; he made it unsafe for others to agree
segments.takeaway: Being right is step one. Making it safe for people to accept they were part of the problem is step two.
segments.challenge: Before sharing an uncomfortable root cause today, write the one sentence that shows respect for the people involved.

source.title: The Doctors' Plague: Germs, Childbed Fever, and the Strange Story of Ignác Semmelweis
source.author: Sherwin B. Nuland

visual.title: Mothers dying of childbed fever, Vienna 1840s
visual.caption: The data was clear. The argument still failed.

script.speaker: host
script.text: Vienna General Hospital, the 1840s. It has two maternity clinics, and women in the city know something the doctors don't want to hear. They beg not to be sent to the first one.

script.speaker: cohost
script.text: Why the first one?

script.speaker: host
script.text: Because in the first clinic, staffed by doctors and medical students, roughly one mother in ten was dying of childbed fever in some years. In the second clinic, staffed by midwives, it was closer to four in a hundred.

script.speaker: cohost
script.text: Same hospital, same city, admissions on alternating days. That's a natural experiment.

script.speaker: host
script.text: And a young Hungarian doctor named Ignaz Semmelweis treats it like one. He rules things out one by one. Birthing position. Ventilation. Even a priest who walked through ringing a bell. Nothing explains it. Then in 1847 his friend Jakob Kolletschka is nicked by a student's scalpel during an autopsy, and dies of something that looks exactly like childbed fever.

script.speaker: cohost
script.text: And the doctors were going straight from the autopsy room to the delivery ward.

script.speaker: host
script.text: Straight from the dead to the living. So Semmelweis has everyone wash their hands in a chlorinated lime solution. Deaths in the first clinic fall to around one or two percent.

script.speaker: cohost
script.text: So he's a hero.

script.speaker: host
script.text: He's ignored. Then mocked. His appointment isn't renewed, and he dies in an asylum in 1865, before germ theory catches up and proves him right.

script.speaker: cohost
script.text: Why wouldn't the data win?

script.speaker: host
script.text: Two reasons, and both are worth stealing. First, his idea meant the doctors themselves were killing their patients. That's an incredibly hard message to receive. Second, he was terrible at delivering it. He waited well over a decade to publish, and then wrote open letters calling his critics murderers.

script.speaker: cohost
script.text: That is a crucial conversation done about as badly as humanly possible.

script.speaker: host
script.text: Pretty much. There's even a name now for reflexively rejecting evidence because it clashes with what everyone believes. The Semmelweis reflex.

script.speaker: cohost
script.text: Every engineer who's found the root cause in someone else's team has felt both sides of this.

script.speaker: host
script.text: Right. Being right is step one. Making it safe for people to accept that they were part of the problem is step two, and that's the step that actually changes anything.

script.speaker: cohost
script.text: Speaking of being part of the problem, let's talk about what happens when the machine flies the plane.

deeperQuestions: When have we rejected good evidence because of who delivered it, or how?
How do our postmortems separate the finding from blame?
What would it take for a junior engineer's uncomfortable data to win an argument here?

segments.title: The Ironies of Automation
segments.summary: Lisanne Bainbridge's 1983 paper argued that automating the routine leaves humans with only the rarest, hardest moments, while their skills fade from disuse. Air France 447 in 2009 showed the cost: a brief sensor fault handed a healthy airliner back to pilots who rarely hand-flew at altitude.
keyPoints: Automation takes the easy work and leaves people the hardest cases
Skills fade exactly where the handoff will demand them
Design for the handoff: practice, explanation, and context
segments.takeaway: The scariest outage isn't the one automation causes. It's the one it hands back to you.
segments.challenge: Name one task your automation now does that nobody on the team has done by hand in a year.

visual.title: The automation trap

items.label: Less hands-on practice
items.detail: People rarely do the task themselves

visual.caption: Design for the handoff, not just the happy path.

script.speaker: host
script.text: In 1983, a cognitive psychologist named Lisanne Bainbridge wrote a short paper with a great title. Ironies of Automation. It's about industrial control rooms, but honestly it reads like it was written about AI ops last week.

script.speaker: cohost
script.text: Okay, what's the irony?

script.speaker: host
script.text: There are a few. The big one is this. We automate the easy, routine parts of a job, and we leave the human to handle whatever the automation can't. Which means the person ends up with only the hardest, rarest situations, while getting less and less practice.

script.speaker: cohost
script.text: So the better the automation, the rustier the person who has to take over when it fails.

script.speaker: host
script.text: Exactly. And they have to take over suddenly, without context, at the worst possible moment.

script.speaker: cohost
script.text: That's Air France 447.

script.speaker: host
script.text: June 2009, over the Atlantic at night. Ice crystals block the airspeed sensors, the autopilot disconnects, and two well trained pilots are suddenly hand flying an airliner at cruise altitude, something they almost never did. The nose goes up, the plane stalls, and it falls for more than three minutes into the ocean. Two hundred and twenty eight people die.

script.speaker: cohost
script.text: And the aircraft itself was basically fine.

script.speaker: host
script.text: Apart from that short burst of bad airspeed data, yes. The investigators pointed to the crew's lack of practice flying by hand at high altitude, and to stall warnings that were confusing in the moment.

script.speaker: cohost
script.text: Okay, map this onto the network. We're adding automation everywhere. Auto remediation, intent based config, AI assistants drafting changes.

script.speaker: host
script.text: And Bainbridge's warning isn't, don't automate. It's, design for the handoff. Keep people in practice with game days and drills. Make the automation show what it's doing and why, so taking over doesn't mean starting from zero. And watch for skills that quietly disappear because nobody has needed them in a year.

script.speaker: cohost
script.text: The scary outage isn't the one automation causes. It's the one it hands back to you.

script.speaker: host
script.text: And our last story is a fresh one, from just a few weeks ago.

deeperQuestions: Which manual skills would our team need in a total automation failure, and when did we last practice them?
Does our automation explain its actions well enough for a human to take over mid-incident?
How should AI-assisted changes be reviewed so reviewers don't become rubber stamps?

segments.title: The Gateway That Looked Unused
segments.summary: On September 4, 2026, Inngest removed an AWS virtual private gateway that appeared inactive to make room for a new connection. It was quietly carrying the live Direct Connect association for their data center, and reattaching it didn't bring that association back, so execution was down for 35 minutes.
keyPoints: AWS allows one virtual private gateway per VPC, forcing a swap
The 'idle' gateway carried the live Direct Connect association
Undo didn't undo: the association had to be rebuilt by hand
segments.takeaway: Prove something is idle with traffic data before you pull it, and know what your rollback really restores.
segments.challenge: For the next thing you plan to remove, write down the evidence that it's unused: flow logs, counters, or routes.

source.title: Incident report for September 4, 2026: Network connectivity issues
source.author: Inngest

visual.title: How a cleanup became an outage

items.label: Gateway looks idle
items.detail: Needed room for a new AWS connection

visual.caption: 35 minutes down. Prove it's idle before you pull it.

script.speaker: host
script.text: Last one, and it's fresh. On September fourth this year, Inngest, a company that runs background jobs and workflows for other developers, had an outage and published a really candid incident report.

script.speaker: cohost
script.text: I love a good postmortem.

script.speaker: host
script.text: They were adding capacity and needed a new private connection into AWS. And AWS only lets you attach one virtual private gateway to a VPC at a time. So to make room, the team removed a gateway that looked inactive.

script.speaker: cohost
script.text: Looked inactive. I can already feel where this is going.

script.speaker: host
script.text: That gateway was quietly carrying the live Direct Connect association for their existing data center. The private path their execution services used to reach state in AWS. At eighteen thirteen UTC, function execution across the platform stopped.

script.speaker: cohost
script.text: Okay, but that's an easy fix. Put it back.

script.speaker: host
script.text: That's what they did, within minutes. They reattached it. And nothing came back.

script.speaker: cohost
script.text: Huh.

script.speaker: host
script.text: Because detaching the gateway had also dropped a separate piece, the association with the Direct Connect gateway. Reattaching didn't restore that automatically. The team had to work out what else had silently gone missing and rebuild it by hand. Thirty five minutes of downtime in total.

script.speaker: cohost
script.text: So it's Three Mile Island in miniature. The console showed what they expected, an idle gateway, not what was actually flowing through it.

script.speaker: host
script.text: And it's the Model 299 too. Nobody forgot how networking works. A dependency just wasn't visible at the moment someone had to make the call. Their fixes are what you'd hope for. Tighter controls on network changes, and redundant paths so one association can't take everything down.

script.speaker: cohost
script.text: My takeaway is a pre-change question. Before I remove anything that looks unused, what's my evidence? Flow logs, route tables, traffic counters. Not the name, not the diagram, and definitely not my memory.

script.speaker: host
script.text: And know what your undo really undoes. Reverting a change doesn't always rebuild everything the change took apart.

script.speaker: cohost
script.text: That's the episode.

script.speaker: host
script.text: Measure the valve. Write the checklist. Make it safe to hear bad news. Keep your hands in practice. And prove something's idle before you pull it. Have a great day.

script.speaker: cohost
script.text: See you tomorrow.

deeperQuestions: Which of our cloud network objects have hidden associations a detach would silently drop?
Do our rollback plans list every object a change touches, or just the main one?
Where do we have a single private path that critical services depend on?
